title: HTTP servers and middleware
summary: The built-in http module, the request and response objects, and how middleware chains such as Express and Koa work underneath.

sections.title: The http module
sections.body:
`http.createServer((req, res) => ...)` calls your handler for every request. `req` is a readable stream with `method`, `url` and lower-cased `headers`; the body must be read from the stream. `res` is a writable stream: set `res.statusCode` and headers, then `res.end(body)`.

Every request must end with exactly one response. Forgetting `res.end()` leaves the client hanging until a timeout; writing headers after the body has started throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`.

sections.title: Middleware
sections.body:
Frameworks split a handler into **middleware**: small functions that each do one job (logging, auth, body parsing, rate limiting) and then pass control on. Express middleware has the shape `(req, res, next)`; calling `next()` runs the next one, `next(err)` jumps to the error handlers.

Koa-style middleware is `async (ctx, next) => {}` and `await next()` returns after everything downstream has finished. That gives an "onion": code before `await next()` runs on the way in, code after it runs on the way out, which is ideal for timing and error handling.

sections.title: Order matters
sections.body:
Middleware runs in the order you register it. Put request ids and logging first, then security headers, body parsing with a size limit, authentication, validation, the route, and finally a single error handler.

A middleware must either respond or call `next` exactly once. Calling `next()` twice runs the rest of the chain twice; calling neither hangs the request.

sections.title: Timeouts and shutdown
sections.body: Set server timeouts (`requestTimeout`, `headersTimeout`, `keepAliveTimeout`) so slow clients cannot hold connections forever. On `SIGTERM`, stop accepting connections with `server.close()`, let in-flight requests finish within a deadline, close database pools, then exit. Containers and orchestrators rely on this graceful shutdown.

pitfalls: Forgetting to end the response on an error path.
Calling `next()` and also sending a response, or calling `next()` twice.
Parsing request bodies without a size limit.
Registering the error handler before the routes.

gotchas.question: How does Express know a middleware is an error handler?
gotchas.answer: By its arity: a function declared with four parameters `(err, req, res, next)` is treated as an error handler and skipped for normal requests. Dropping the unused `next` parameter silently turns it back into a normal middleware.

gotchas.question: Why might `await next()` in a Koa middleware not catch an error from an Express-style callback?
gotchas.answer: Errors thrown later in a callback (for example inside `setTimeout` or an emitter listener) are not part of the promise that `next()` returns. Only errors thrown synchronously or as rejections of awaited promises flow back up the chain.

gotchas.question: What is the difference between `res.write` and `res.end`?
gotchas.answer: `write` sends a chunk and keeps the response open (chunked transfer). `end` optionally sends a final chunk and finishes the response. Headers are sent with the first `write` or with `end`.
